column4: Last lesson you learned to protect the money first: risk one to two percent, set the stop before you enter, demand more reward than risk. Rules on paper are easy. Following them with money on the line is not. Here is the truth most courses skip: the hardest part of investing is not the charts, it is the person holding the phone. That is you. Fear and greed will try to run your money, and they are convincing. This lesson hands you the two tools that beat them every time: a written plan, and an honest journal. That is the discipline that separates an investor from a gambler.

Meet the two villains. When a stock is ripping and everyone is hyped, greed whispers buy now, do not miss out, so you buy near the top. Then when it drops and the mood turns dark, fear screams sell, get out, so you sell near the bottom. Buy high, sell low, the exact opposite of a good plan. Emotional resilience does not mean feeling nothing. It means accepting that swings are normal and refusing to let a loud feeling place the order.

Here is the fix, and it is almost boringly simple. Decide your entry, your exit, and your stop before you click anything. Watch the two lines on screen. The red one is the emotional trader, whipsawed, buying the top and selling the bottom. The green one is you with a plan, climbing calmly through the same noise. This is illustrative, not a forecast. But when the plan is written down first, fear and greed do not get a vote.

Now your secret weapon, and it costs nothing: the journal. For every trade, write five things. Why you got in. Your plan. Your exit. Your stop. And what actually happened. Then, and this is the part most people skip, read it back. The journal is a mirror. It shows the mistakes you keep repeating and the setups that genuinely work for you. Reviewed honestly, it is the best coach you will ever have.

Your turn. Drag the dial from extreme fear all the way to extreme greed. At each point, notice what the emotional move would be, and right beside it, what your written plan would say instead. Feel the gap between the two. That gap is exactly where discipline lives.
Now sort these. Some are plan moves, calm and deliberate. Some are feelings moves, driven by fear or greed. Tap a card, then drop it in the right column, and let it sink in which is which.
Five quick questions. Show me you can keep your head and trust the plan.

That is the inner game. Fear and greed will always show up, but a written plan and an honest journal keep them from running your money. And remember, a small loss is a win, because it protects your capital for the next opportunity.
